articles.title: RCD protection for socket-outlets
articles.text: Socket-outlets rated up to 32 A on AC final circuits need additional protection from an RCD with a rated trip current of 30 mA or less. Amendment 2 rewrote the rule in three groups (everyday users, other locations, and mobile equipment used outdoors); only the other-locations group can be left out, and only after a documented risk assessment.

articles.title: RCD protection for domestic lighting circuits
articles.text: In domestic (household) premises, AC final circuits that supply luminaires need additional protection from an RCD of 30 mA or less.

articles.title: Arc fault detection devices (AFDD)
articles.text: An AFDD detects dangerous arcing in a final circuit. Amendment 2 recommends AFDDs on single-phase AC circuits that feed socket-outlets up to 32 A, and trade sources describe them as required in higher-risk residential buildings, houses in multiple occupation, student accommodation and care homes. The sources disagree on the exact wording, so the current text needs checking.

articles.title: Consumer unit enclosure
articles.text: In domestic premises, consumer units and similar boards follow BS EN 61439-3 and are either made of non-combustible material (steel counts) or housed in a non-combustible cabinet.

articles.title: Earthing arrangements: TN-S, TN-C-S and TT
articles.text: The supply's earthing arrangement decides how a fault is cleared. TN-S: the supplier provides a separate earth. TN-C-S (also called PME): the supplier combines neutral and earth, so the installation's earth comes from the neutral. TT: the installation uses its own earth electrode, so RCD protection is needed to clear faults.

articles.title: Main protective bonding
articles.text: Extraneous metal that enters the building, such as gas and water service pipes and structural steel, is bonded to the main earthing terminal so touch voltages stay low if a fault occurs.

articles.title: Main bonding conductor size
articles.text: The size of the main bonding conductor follows from the size of the supply neutral or earthing conductor. The usual copper minimum is 6 mm2 and the maximum 25 mm2, and 10 mm2 is common on PME supplies. The table that fixes the sizes is copyrighted and is not reproduced.

articles.title: Supplementary bonding in bathrooms
articles.text: Extra bonding between metal parts in a room with a bath or shower can be left out only if all circuits there have RCD protection and automatic disconnection, and all incoming metal is already main-bonded.

articles.title: Circuit protective conductor size
articles.text: Size the circuit protective conductor (cpc) either by the adiabatic equation, which limits heating during a fault, or from a simplified table that relates it to the line conductor size. The table is copyrighted and is not reproduced.

articles.title: Earthing conductor and main earthing terminal
articles.text: The earthing conductor runs from the main earthing terminal to the earth electrode or the supplier's earth terminal. It must be sized, protected against corrosion and mechanical damage, and connected at the main earthing terminal.

articles.title: Earth electrodes for TT systems
articles.text: A TT installation relies on its own earth electrode (a rod or pipe, tape or wire, or plate) and on RCD protection. The electrode resistance multiplied by the RCD trip current must stay at or below 50 V.

articles.title: Overload protection and cable coordination
articles.text: The protective device rating must sit between the circuit's design current and the cable's current-carrying capacity (Ib <= In <= Iz), and the device's guaranteed tripping current must not exceed 1.45 times the cable capacity.

articles.title: Short-circuit protection
articles.text: The device must clear a short circuit before the cable overheats: the cable's heat-withstand limit must be higher than the let-through energy of the device.

articles.title: Dividing an installation into circuits
articles.text: The installation is divided into several circuits so that a fault affects as little as possible, safe maintenance is possible and nuisance tripping is limited. The UK has no fixed list of dedicated circuits like the North American rule.

articles.title: Maximum demand
articles.text: The designer assesses the maximum demand, with diversity, to size the supply and the conductors. The standard diversity tables are in industry guidance, not in the regulations themselves.

articles.title: Current-carrying capacity and derating
articles.text: A cable's current-carrying capacity depends on how it is installed, the ambient temperature, grouping with other circuits and thermal insulation. The capacity tables are in Appendix 4 and are copyrighted, so the figures are not reproduced.

articles.title: Voltage drop
articles.text: Voltage drop from the origin of the installation to the load must stay within the limits in Appendix 12, commonly given as 3 percent for lighting and 5 percent for other circuits on a 230 V public supply.

articles.title: Isolation and switching, and the main switch
articles.text: Every installation can be isolated by a main switch at its origin that opens all live conductors, and each circuit or item of equipment has isolation and switching suited to its use. The main switch must be accessible and isolators can be secured against being switched on by mistake.

articles.title: Circuit charts and schedules
articles.text: A durable, legible chart, diagram or schedule at each consumer unit or distribution board shows the type and make-up of every circuit. In homes, the schedule from the electrical certificate fixed at the board usually meets this.

articles.title: RCD test notice
articles.text: A notice at the consumer unit tells users to press the RCD test button every six months.

articles.title: Conductor colours
articles.text: Single-phase installations use brown for the line, blue for the neutral and green-and-yellow for the circuit protective conductor; three-phase installations use brown, black and grey for the lines.

articles.title: Cables concealed in walls and partitions
articles.text: A cable concealed less than 50 mm below a wall surface must run in a safe zone (vertical and horizontal runs tied to accessories and corners) and have 30 mA RCD protection, unless it has another protection listed in 522.6.204.

articles.title: Alternatives to RCD protection for concealed cables
articles.text: A concealed cable can avoid the RCD requirement if it has an earthed metal sheath or earthed conduit or trunking, is protected against nails and screws by its construction or an earthed barrier, or is a SELV or PELV circuit.

articles.title: Bathrooms and shower rooms
articles.text: A room with a bath or shower is divided into zones. Zone 0 is inside the bath or shower tray, zone 1 is above it up to 2.25 m, and zone 2 extends 0.6 m beyond zone 1. Only very low voltage (SELV) equipment is allowed in zone 0. Socket-outlets other than shaver units are not allowed in zones 0 to 2, and IP ratings and RCD protection apply across the zones.

articles.title: Swimming pools and basins
articles.text: A swimming pool is divided into zones 0, 1 and 2. Zone 0 is the basin itself, where only very low voltage (SELV) equipment is allowed. Equipment and wiring in the other zones follow zone rules, and metal parts in zones 0 to 2 are supplementary-bonded.

articles.title: Supplementary bonding at pools
articles.text: Extraneous conductive parts and exposed conductive parts in the pool zones, such as metal ladders and rails, are connected together by a supplementary bonding conductor.

articles.title: Electric vehicle charging points
articles.text: Each charging point needs 30 mA RCD protection plus protection against residual direct current (a Type B RCD, or a Type A or F RCD with a 6 mA residual direct current detecting device). Special rules limit the use of a PME earth for outdoor charging points. Amendment 4 reportedly changes the residual direct current wording, so the current text needs checking.

articles.title: Accessibility and maintenance
articles.text: Equipment is installed so that it can be reached for operating, inspecting, testing and maintaining. The regulations give no fixed clearance dimensions; a duty to provide adequate working space comes from the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989.

articles.title: Workmanship and materials
articles.text: Installation work is carried out by competent people with proper materials, and connections are secure, suitable for the conductor and accessible for inspection.
